name: Standard Normal PDF
description: Computes the probability density of the standard normal distribution at a given z-score, using exp(-z^2/2) divided by the square root of 2 pi. It gives the height of the bell curve at that point, which peaks at about 0.3989 when z is 0.
notes: This is a density (curve height), not a probability; probabilities come from the area under the curve. The distribution has mean 0 and standard deviation 1, and is symmetric in z.

name: Log-Normal Distribution PDF
description: Computes the probability density of the log-normal distribution at a value x, where the natural log of x is normally distributed with the given log-mean and log-standard deviation. The result is the height of the skewed density curve at x.
notes: The value x must be strictly positive, and mu and sigma describe the distribution of ln(x), not of x itself. The distribution is right-skewed and models quantities that cannot be negative.

name: Weibull Distribution CDF
description: Computes the cumulative distribution function of the Weibull distribution at x, as one minus exp(-(x/lambda)^k). It gives the probability that a Weibull-distributed variable, such as a time to failure, is at most x.
notes: Valid for x at least 0, with positive scale (lambda) and shape (k) parameters; the result is a probability between 0 and 1. The shape k governs whether failure rate increases (k>1), stays constant (k=1), or decreases (k<1).

name: Weibull Distribution PDF
description: Computes the probability density of the Weibull distribution at x, as (k/lambda)(x/lambda)^(k-1) times exp(-(x/lambda)^k). It gives the height of the Weibull density curve, widely used to model lifetimes and reliability.
notes: Valid for x at least 0, with positive scale (lambda) and shape (k) parameters; this is a density, not a probability. With k = 2 the Weibull reduces to the Rayleigh distribution.

name: Weibull Hazard Function
description: Computes the Weibull hazard (failure rate) function at time x, as (k/lambda)(x/lambda)^(k-1). It gives the instantaneous rate of failure at time x given survival up to that time, central to reliability engineering.
notes: The shape k determines the trend: k>1 gives an increasing (wear-out) hazard, k=1 a constant hazard, and k<1 a decreasing (infant-mortality) hazard. Scale (lambda) and shape (k) must be positive and x at least 0.

name: Rayleigh Distribution PDF
description: Computes the probability density of the Rayleigh distribution at x, as (x/sigma^2) times exp(-x^2/(2 sigma^2)). It models the magnitude of a two-dimensional vector whose components are independent zero-mean normals, such as wind speed or signal envelopes.
notes: Valid for x at least 0 with positive scale sigma; this is a density, not a probability. The Rayleigh distribution is the special case of the Weibull with shape parameter 2.

name: Rayleigh Distribution CDF
description: Gives the cumulative probability that a Rayleigh-distributed variable is at most x, computed as 1 minus exp(-x^2/(2*sigma^2)). The Rayleigh distribution models the magnitude of a two-dimensional vector whose components are independent zero-mean Gaussians with scale sigma.
notes: Valid only for x greater than or equal to 0; sigma must be positive. The scale sigma is the Gaussian component standard deviation, not the distribution mean, which equals sigma*sqrt(pi/2).

name: Gumbel Distribution PDF
description: Evaluates the probability density of the Gumbel (extreme value type I) distribution at x, given location mu and scale beta. It is widely used to model the distribution of maxima such as annual peak floods or extreme wind speeds.
notes: beta must be positive. This is the maximum (right-skewed) Gumbel form; the minimum form uses a sign-flipped exponent. The location mu is the mode, not the mean.

name: Gumbel Distribution CDF
description: Gives the cumulative probability that a Gumbel-distributed variable is at most x, computed as exp(-exp(-(x-mu)/beta)) with location mu and scale beta. It represents the probability that an extreme maximum does not exceed x.
notes: beta must be positive. This is the maximum form; the return probability (exceedance) is 1 minus this value. mu shifts the curve and beta controls its spread.

name: Logistic Distribution PDF
description: Evaluates the probability density of the logistic distribution at x, given location mu and scale s. Its bell shape resembles a normal distribution but has heavier tails, and it is symmetric about the mean mu.
notes: s must be positive and is proportional to the standard deviation (sd = s*pi/sqrt(3)), not equal to it. The density peaks at x = mu with value 1/(4*s).

name: Logistic Distribution CDF
description: Gives the cumulative probability that a logistic variable is at most x, computed as 1/(1+exp(-(x-mu)/s)) with location mu and scale s. This is the standard logistic (sigmoid) curve underlying logistic regression.
notes: s must be positive. The value equals 0.5 at x = mu and increases monotonically from 0 to 1. Larger s makes the transition more gradual.

name: Pareto Distribution PDF
description: Evaluates the probability density of the Pareto distribution at x, computed as alpha*xm^alpha/x^(alpha+1) with minimum value xm and shape alpha. It models heavy-tailed quantities such as wealth, city sizes, and file lengths.
notes: Defined only for x greater than or equal to xm; both xm and alpha must be positive. Smaller alpha means a heavier tail; the mean is finite only when alpha is greater than 1.

name: Pareto Distribution CDF
description: Gives the cumulative probability that a Pareto variable is at most x, computed as 1-(xm/x)^alpha with minimum value xm and shape alpha. It represents the fraction of the population falling below the level x.
notes: Defined only for x greater than or equal to xm; xm and alpha must be positive. The complementary value (xm/x)^alpha is the tail probability of exceeding x.

name: Laplace Distribution PDF
description: Evaluates the probability density of the Laplace (double exponential) distribution at x, computed as exp(-|x-mu|/b)/(2*b) with location mu and scale b. It has a sharp peak at mu and exponentially decaying symmetric tails.
notes: b must be positive. The peak density is 1/(2*b) at x = mu, and the variance equals 2*b^2. Its heavier peak distinguishes it from the normal distribution.

name: Cauchy Distribution PDF
description: Evaluates the probability density of the Cauchy (Lorentzian) distribution at x, computed as 1/(pi*gam*(1+((x-x0)/gam)^2)) with location x0 and scale gam. It is a symmetric bell-shaped curve with very heavy tails.
notes: gam must be positive. The Cauchy distribution has no defined mean or variance; x0 is the median and mode, and gam is the half-width at half-maximum.

name: Cauchy Distribution CDF
description: Gives the cumulative probability that a Cauchy variable is at most x, computed as 1/2+atan((x-x0)/gam)/pi with location x0 and scale gam. It maps any real x smoothly onto a probability between 0 and 1.
notes: gam must be positive and atan returns radians. The value equals 0.5 at x = x0; because the tails are heavy, the curve approaches 0 and 1 slowly.

name: Exponential Distribution CDF
description: Gives the probability that an exponentially distributed waiting time is at most x, computed as 1-exp(-lam*x) with rate lam. It models the time until the first event in a Poisson process, such as time to failure.
notes: Requires x greater than or equal to 0 and rate lam positive; the product lam*x must be dimensionless, so lam is in 1/s when x is in seconds. The mean waiting time is 1/lam.

name: Exponential Survival Function
description: Gives the probability that an exponentially distributed lifetime exceeds time x, computed as exp(-lam*x) with rate lam. This survival (reliability) function is the complement of the exponential CDF.
notes: Requires x greater than or equal to 0 and rate lam positive, with lam*x dimensionless. Because of the memoryless property, the survival probability over any future interval does not depend on elapsed time.

name: Poisson Probability P(0)
description: Gives the probability of observing zero events in a Poisson process with mean count lam, computed as exp(-lam). This is the chance that nothing happens in the interval over which lam counts are expected on average.
notes: lam must be non-negative and represents the expected number of events over the interval, not a rate per unit time unless the interval is one unit. As lam grows, this probability drops rapidly.

name: Poisson Probability P(1)
description: Gives the probability of observing exactly one event in a Poisson process with mean count lam, computed as lam*exp(-lam). It is the second term of the Poisson probability mass function.
notes: lam must be non-negative and is the expected count over the interval. This probability is maximized at lam = 1, where it equals about 0.368.

name: Poisson Probability P(2)
description: Gives the probability of observing exactly two events in a Poisson process with mean count lam, computed as lam^2*exp(-lam)/2. It is the third term of the Poisson probability mass function.
notes: lam must be non-negative and is the expected count over the interval. The denominator 2 is the factorial 2! from the general formula lam^k*exp(-lam)/k!.

name: Geometric Distribution Mean
description: Gives the expected number of independent trials needed to obtain the first success, computed as 1/p where p is the per-trial success probability. It is the mean of the geometric distribution counting trials.
notes: p must be strictly between 0 and 1. This uses the trials-until-first-success convention, so the result is always at least 1; the failures-before-success convention gives (1-p)/p instead.

name: Geometric Distribution Variance
description: Gives the variance of the number of trials until the first success in independent Bernoulli trials, computed as (1-p)/p^2 with success probability p. It quantifies the spread of the waiting time to success.
notes: p must be strictly between 0 and 1. This matches the trials-until-first-success convention; the variance is the same under the failures-before-success convention.

name: Negative Binomial Mean
description: Gives the expected number of failures before achieving r successes in independent Bernoulli trials, computed as r*(1-p)/p with per-trial success probability p. It generalizes the geometric mean to r successes.
notes: p must be strictly between 0 and 1 and r positive. This counts failures before the r-th success; the total number of trials has mean r/p instead.

name: Negative Binomial Variance
description: Gives the variance of the number of failures before achieving r successes in independent Bernoulli trials, computed as r*(1-p)/p^2 with success probability p. It measures the dispersion of the failure count.
notes: p must be strictly between 0 and 1 and r positive. Because the variance exceeds the mean r*(1-p)/p, the distribution is overdispersed relative to Poisson.

name: Hypergeometric Distribution Mean
description: Gives the expected number of successes when drawing n items without replacement from a population of size N containing K successes, computed as n*K/N. It equals the sample size times the population success fraction.
notes: All counts should be non-negative integers with n and K at most N. Sampling is without replacement, so the mean matches the binomial mean n*K/N but the variance is smaller.

name: Bernoulli Variance
description: Gives the variance of a single Bernoulli trial with success probability p, computed as p*(1-p). It measures the uncertainty of a binary outcome and underlies the variance of binomial counts.
notes: p must lie between 0 and 1. The variance is maximized at p = 0.5, where it equals 0.25, and vanishes when the outcome is certain (p = 0 or p = 1).

name: Continuous Uniform Distribution Mean
description: Gives the mean of a continuous uniform distribution on the interval [a, b], computed as the midpoint (a+b)/2. Every value in the interval is equally likely, so the average is its center.
notes: Requires b greater than or equal to a. The result is the midpoint regardless of interval width; the spread is described separately by the variance (b-a)^2/12.

name: Gamma Distribution Mean
description: Gives the mean of a gamma distribution with shape k and scale theta, computed as k*theta. The gamma distribution models positive continuous quantities such as waiting times for multiple Poisson events.
notes: k and theta must be positive. This uses the shape-scale parameterization; with the shape-rate form the mean is k/beta, where beta = 1/theta.

name: Gamma Distribution Variance
description: Gives the variance of a gamma distribution with shape k and scale theta, computed as k*theta^2. It measures the dispersion of the gamma-distributed quantity around its mean k*theta.
notes: k and theta must be positive. In the shape-rate parameterization this becomes k/beta^2, where beta = 1/theta. The variance grows with the square of the scale.

name: Beta Distribution Mean
description: Gives the mean of a beta distribution with shape parameters alpha and beta, computed as alpha/(alpha+beta). The beta distribution models probabilities and proportions bounded between 0 and 1.
notes: alpha and beta must both be positive. The result always lies strictly between 0 and 1, and equals 0.5 when alpha equals beta (symmetric case).

name: Beta Distribution Variance
description: Gives the variance of a beta distribution with shape parameters alpha and beta, computed as alpha*beta/((alpha+beta)^2*(alpha+beta+1)). It quantifies the spread of a proportion around its mean alpha/(alpha+beta).
notes: alpha and beta must both be positive. Larger alpha+beta (more concentration) reduces the variance, so the distribution tightens as the effective sample size increases.

name: Fisher z-Transformation
description: Transforms a Pearson correlation coefficient r into the Fisher z value 0.5*ln((1+r)/(1-r)), which is approximately normally distributed. This stabilizes the variance so correlations can be tested and averaged.
notes: r must be strictly between -1 and 1; values at the boundaries make the logarithm diverge. The transform equals the inverse hyperbolic tangent, artanh(r).

name: Log-Odds (Logit)
description: Converts a probability p into its log-odds (logit), computed as ln(p/(1-p)). This maps a probability from the range 0 to 1 onto the whole real line and is the link function of logistic regression.
notes: p must be strictly between 0 and 1. The logit is 0 at p = 0.5, negative below it, and positive above; the inverse is the sigmoid 1/(1+exp(-x)).

name: Softmax (Two-Class)
description: Converts two logits a and b into the probability of class A, computed as exp(a)/(exp(a)+exp(b)). This is the two-class softmax, which normalizes the exponentiated scores into a probability that sums to one across the classes.
notes: Only the difference a-b matters, so the result equals the sigmoid 1/(1+exp(-(a-b))). The probability of class B is one minus this value.

name: Normal CDF (Logistic Approximation)
description: Approximates the standard normal cumulative distribution at z using the logistic function 1/(1+exp(-1.702*z)). The constant 1.702 is chosen so the logistic curve closely matches the normal CDF.
notes: This is an approximation, accurate to within about 0.01 in probability; use an exact normal CDF when high precision is required. z is a standardized (mean 0, sd 1) score.

name: Markov's Inequality Bound
description: Gives Markov's inequality upper bound on the probability that a non-negative random variable reaches at least a, computed as mu/a from the mean mu. It bounds tail probability using only the mean.
notes: Valid only for non-negative variables with a positive; the bound is meaningful only when a exceeds mu, otherwise it exceeds 1. It is often loose because it ignores variance.

name: Expected Value (Two-Outcome Gamble)
description: Gives the expected value of a gamble with two outcomes, computed as p*a+(1-p)*b where payoff a occurs with probability p and payoff b otherwise. It is the probability-weighted average payoff.
notes: p must be between 0 and 1. The result shares the units of the payoffs a and b and represents a long-run average, not a guaranteed single-trial outcome.

name: Variance (Two-Outcome Distribution)
description: Gives the variance of a two-outcome random variable taking value a with probability p and value b otherwise, computed as p*(1-p)*(a-b)^2. It measures the spread of the two possible outcomes.
notes: p must be between 0 and 1. The variance depends only on the gap a-b and equals the Bernoulli variance p*(1-p) scaled by the squared difference.

name: Kelly Criterion Optimal Fraction
description: Gives the Kelly-optimal fraction of bankroll to wager, computed as (b*p-(1-p))/b where b is the net odds and p the win probability. It maximizes the expected long-run logarithmic growth of capital.
notes: b and p must be positive with p between 0 and 1. A negative result means the bet has no edge and should be avoided; the numerator is the expected net return per unit staked.

name: Parametric Value at Risk (Normal)
description: Gives the parametric Value at Risk return threshold under a normal assumption, computed as mu-z*sigma from the mean return mu, quantile z, and volatility sigma. It is the return level not expected to be breached at the chosen confidence.
notes: z is the standard normal quantile for the confidence level (e.g. 1.645 for 95 percent). The result is a return; multiply by portfolio value to get a monetary VaR. A negative result denotes a loss.

name: Series System Reliability (Two Components)
description: Gives the reliability of a two-component series system, computed as r1*r2 from the component reliabilities r1 and r2. The system works only if both components work, assuming independent failures.
notes: r1 and r2 are probabilities between 0 and 1 and are assumed statistically independent. The series reliability is always less than or equal to each component's reliability.

name: Parallel System Reliability (Two Components)
description: Gives the reliability of a two-component parallel (redundant) system, computed as 1-(1-r1)*(1-r2) from the component reliabilities r1 and r2. The system fails only if both components fail, assuming independence.
notes: r1 and r2 are probabilities between 0 and 1 and are assumed independent. The parallel reliability is always greater than or equal to each component's reliability, reflecting the benefit of redundancy.

name: Birthday Problem Approximation
description: Approximates the probability that at least two of n people share a birthday among N equally likely days, computed as 1-exp(-n^2/(2*N)). It gives the surprisingly high chance of a coincidence in a group.
notes: This is an approximation valid when n is much smaller than N; it slightly overestimates the exact value. Birthdays are assumed uniformly and independently distributed over N days.

name: One-Sample Proportion Z-Statistic
description: Gives the z-statistic for testing a sample proportion phat against a hypothesized proportion p0, computed as (phat-p0)/sqrt(p0*(1-p0)/n) with sample size n. It measures how many standard errors the estimate lies from the null value.
notes: Proportions must be between 0 and 1 and n large enough for the normal approximation (roughly n*p0 and n*(1-p0) both at least 5). The standard error uses the null proportion p0, not phat.

name: Standard Error of Skewness
description: Gives the standard error of the sample skewness for a sample of size n, computed as sqrt(6*n*(n-1)/((n-2)*(n+1)*(n+3))). It is used to judge whether an observed skewness differs significantly from zero.
notes: Requires n greater than 2. Compare the sample skewness to roughly plus or minus twice this value; the formula assumes independent observations from a normal population.

name: Margin of Error (Normal)
description: Gives the margin of error for a mean under a normal model, computed as z*sigma/sqrt(n) from the critical value z, standard deviation sigma, and sample size n. It is the half-width of the confidence interval around the sample mean.
notes: z is the standard normal critical value for the confidence level (e.g. 1.96 for 95 percent). This assumes a known sigma; with an estimated standard deviation use a t critical value instead.

name: Sample Size for a Proportion
description: Gives the sample size needed to estimate a proportion within a target margin of error, computed as z^2*p*(1-p)/moe^2 from the critical value z, estimated proportion p, and margin moe. Larger precision demands a larger sample.
notes: p and moe must be between 0 and 1. Use p = 0.5 for the most conservative (largest) sample size when p is unknown; round the result up to the next whole number.

name: Attributable Risk (Risk Difference)
description: Gives the attributable risk (risk difference), computed as p1-p2 from the risk p1 in the exposed group and p2 in the unexposed group. It is the excess disease risk attributable to the exposure.
notes: p1 and p2 are probabilities between 0 and 1. A positive result indicates increased risk from exposure and a negative result a protective effect; it is an absolute, not relative, measure.

name: Standard Error of Difference (Two Means)
description: Gives the standard error of the difference between two independent sample means, computed as sqrt(s1^2/n1+s2^2/n2) from the group standard deviations s1, s2 and sample sizes n1, n2. It scales the difference in a two-sample z or t test.
notes: The two samples are assumed independent; this unpooled form does not require equal variances (the Welch approach). s1 and s2 are standard deviations, not variances.

name: Univariate Mahalanobis Distance
description: Gives the univariate Mahalanobis distance of an observation x from a mean mu, computed as |x-mu|/sigma with standard deviation sigma. In one dimension it equals the absolute standard (z) score, expressing distance in standard deviations.
notes: sigma must be positive. In one dimension this reduces to the absolute z-score; the general multivariate form uses the covariance matrix instead of a single sigma.

name: Chi-Squared Cell Statistic
description: Gives the chi-squared contribution of a single cell, computed as (obs-ex)^2/ex from the observed frequency obs and expected frequency ex. Summing this over all cells yields the Pearson chi-squared test statistic.
notes: The expected frequency ex must be positive and is typically at least 5 for the chi-squared approximation to hold. Frequencies are counts, not proportions or percentages.

name: Conditional Probability P(A|B)
description: Computes the conditional probability of event A given event B, P(A|B), from the joint probability P(A∩B) and the marginal probability P(B). The result represents the probability that A occurs given that B has already occurred.
notes: Requires P(B) > 0; both pab and pb must lie within the valid probability range [0, 1], and pab cannot exceed pb.

name: Expected Value of a Linear Transformation E(aX+b)
description: Computes the expected value of a linear transformation aX+b of a random variable X, using the linearity of expectation. The result represents the mean of the transformed random variable.
notes: Valid for any random variable X with finite mean mu = E(X); a and b are constants and mu must already be computed or known beforehand.

name: Variance of a Linear Transformation Var(aX+b)
description: Computes the variance of a linear transformation aX+b of a random variable X, using the property that adding a constant does not change variance while scaling by a multiplies the variance by a². The result represents the variance of the transformed random variable.
notes: Valid for any random variable X with finite variance; sigma must be entered as the standard deviation of X, not the variance itself.
